podcast.title: Pye Records' First Stereo Disks (May 1958)
podcast.body: An English record label named Pye is credited with potentially being the first to release commercial stereo disks in May 1958. This marked an early commercial entry into the stereo LP market. "An English label called Pi may have been the first to release stereo disks in May 1958."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Chronically Underfunded and Trend-Chasing Strategy
podcast.body: Pye was chronically underfunded and, when an artist achieved success, tended to push them to produce as many singles as possible, chasing trends rather than investing in long-term career development. "Pi was chronically underfunded, and when they signed an artist who managed to have any success, they would tend to push that out. The artist to keep producing as many singles as possible, chasing trends, rather than investing in their long-term career survival."

podcast.title: Insistence on Releasing Original "You Really Got Me"
podcast.body: Pye Records was "insistent" on releasing Shell Tauhmey's initial recording of "You Really Got Me," despite Ray Davis's strong dislike for it and his belief that it was overproduced. The label held firmly to their contract, indicating their intent to "put this record out whatever the performers said" until management intervened. "Pai were insistent, they had a contract, and they were going to put this record out whatever the performers said."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Market Share Comparison
podcast.body: EMI and Decca collectively held about 85% of the British record market, dwarfing Pye's share. "EMI and Decker between them had something like 85% of the market, and basically were the record industry in Britain at the time."

podcast.title: Origins in Petula Clark's Career
podcast.body: The company was formed from the merger of two other companies, one of which was specifically established to issue Petula Clark's records. "Indeed the company had been formed from the merger of two other companies, one of which had been formed specifically to issue Clark's records."

podcast.title: Quick Album Demand Post-Hit
podcast.body: Following the sudden smash hit success of "You Really Got Me," Pye Records "quickly exercised their option," demanding that The Kinks record an entire album by the end of August 1964. This rush led to a "patchy affair" composed mostly of R&B covers for their debut album. "Pai records quickly exercised their option, so quickly that the group needed to get an album recorded by the end of August."

podcast.title: Released The Viper's First Single
podcast.body: Pye Records released "Don't You Rock Me Daddy-O" by The Viper's Skiffle Group, which was produced by George Martin. "That recording was on par with on records, and was produced by a young producer who normally did comedy and novelty records, named George Martin."

podcast.title: Signing of The Kinks
podcast.body: Pye Records signed The Kinks (then called The Ravens) to a three-single deal after the group had been rejected by Decca, EMI, and Philips. Pye was also the label for The Searchers and released The Kingsmen's "Louie Louie" in the UK, making it a relevant connection for The Kinks. "when the bid default ended up recording for Pie records, the same label as the searchers."

podcast.title: Third or Fourth Biggest British Label (Early 1960s)
podcast.body: Pye Records was the third or fourth largest record label in Britain during the early 1960s, though significantly smaller than EMI and Decca. "Pi was the third or fourth biggest record label in Britain at the time, but that was a relative matter."
